importing.h1: Importing fresh fish from Egypt: HS codes, documents and cold chain
importing.intro: This guide is for importers, wholesalers and distributors who are planning to buy fresh, chilled whole fish from Egypt. It covers the tariff codes for our 12 main species, the documents a shipment usually needs, the extra steps for the European Union and the basics of keeping fish cold on the way.
importing.disclaimer: This guide gives general information. It is not legal or customs advice. Rules change, so confirm the current requirements with your customs broker and the authorities of the importing country before you ship.

hs.title: HS codes for fresh whole fish
hs.intro_1: Fresh or chilled whole fish is classified under heading 0302 of the Harmonized System (HS), the nomenclature maintained by the World Customs Organization. The first six digits are the same in every country. Fillets (heading 0304) and frozen fish (heading 0303) have different codes.
hs.intro_2: The European Union adds two digits to make the eight-digit Combined Nomenclature (CN) code, and the TARIC database adds two more for EU measures. Other countries add their own national digits after the first six.
hs.table_caption: Fresh or chilled whole fish, heading 0302

notes.other_fish: Not named in a specific subheading, so it falls under 0302.89 "Other"; in the EU, under CN 0302 89 90.
notes.freshwater_other: Its genus is not one of the catfish named in 0302.72, so it falls under 0302.89 "Other"; in the EU, as a freshwater fish, under CN 0302 89 10.

hs.after: Codes checked against the WCO HS 2022 nomenclature and the EU TARIC on {date}. The importer's customs declarant is responsible for the final classification. Duty rates and preferences change, so check the importing country's tariff (for the EU, TARIC or Access2Markets) before you calculate a landed price.

docs.title: Documents for a fresh fish shipment
docs.intro: The exact list depends on the destination. These are the documents usually involved in a fresh fish shipment from Egypt, with EU rules as the main example.

invoice.title: Commercial invoice
invoice.text: Issued by the exporter. It names the seller and buyer and lists the species, HS code, quantity, net weight, value, currency and Incoterm. Customs at destination uses it to assess duty.

packing_list.title: Packing list
packing_list.text: Box-by-box detail: number of boxes, net and gross weight, species and weight grade and box marks. It lets the airline, the border post and the buyer check the consignment.

health_certificate.title: Official health certificate
health_certificate.text: Signed by the competent authority of the exporting country. For the EU, fresh fish for human consumption travels with the model certificate FISH-CRUST-HC, issued through TRACES. The EU accepts it only when the country is listed for the product. In October 2026 the EU listed Egypt for farmed (aquaculture) finfish and crustaceans (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2228), and the establishment that prepares the fish must also be on the EU list of approved establishments. Other markets have their own certificate models.

origin.title: Certificate of origin
origin.text: Most buyers and customs authorities ask for proof that the fish is of Egyptian origin. For the EU, Egyptian goods can qualify for preferential tariff treatment under the EU–Egypt Association Agreement, with a EUR.1 or EUR-MED movement certificate or an origin declaration. Check the rules for your product in Access2Markets.

catch.title: Catch certificate or aquaculture records
catch.text: The EU requires a validated catch certificate for wild-caught sea fish under its IUU Regulation. Aquaculture products obtained from fry or larvae are excluded, and so are fresh tilapia, catfish and carp (0302 71 to 0302 73) and other freshwater fish (0302 89 10). Since 10 January 2026, EU importers submit catch certificates through the CATCH IT system. For farmed fish, ask your supplier for the farm and batch details that link each box to its source.

ched.title: CHED-P pre-notification in TRACES
ched.text: Before the fish arrives, the EU importer or their agent pre-notifies the consignment to the chosen border control post with a Common Health Entry Document for products (CHED-P) in TRACES. The border control post makes documentary, identity and physical checks before the fish is released.

labelling.title: Labelling for EU buyers
labelling.text: Fish offered to consumers or mass caterers in the EU must show the commercial and scientific name, the production method (caught or farmed), the catch or production area and the other information listed in Article 35 of Regulation (EU) No 1379/2013. Agree the box labels with your supplier before the first shipment.

cold.title: Cold-chain basics
cold.intro: Fresh fish is perishable, so temperature control matters at every step from the farm to the buyer's warehouse. EU hygiene rules require fresh fishery products to be kept at a temperature approaching that of melting ice during storage and transport.

temperature.title: Keep it close to 0°C
temperature.text: In practice, exporters work to a 0–4°C range. Fish should be chilled as soon as possible after harvest and stay chilled through grading, packing, the airport and the last mile.

ice.title: Ice
ice.text: Whole fish is packed with ice so it stays at melting-ice temperature. Re-ice as often as needed during storage.

boxes.title: Insulated EPS boxes
boxes.text: Expanded polystyrene (EPS) boxes insulate the fish and are widely used for air freight. Seal and label every box, and check your airline's rules for perishable cargo.

handovers.title: Handovers
handovers.text: Temperature breaks usually happen at handovers: trucks, airport cargo terminals and the border control post. Plan bookings so the fish spends as little time as possible out of the cold, and keep temperature records.

arrival.title: On arrival
arrival.text: Check the fish temperature, the ice and the condition of the boxes, and record any problem with photos before you sign for the delivery.

cold.azafco: How AZAFCO ships: whole fish packed on ice in EPS boxes, moved in our own refrigerated trucks, then by air or road freight.
